Comedia famosa de Don Lope de Cardona

Félix Lope de Vega y Carpio — EMOTHE0236_ComediaFamosaDeDonLopeDeCardona

Hablan en ella las personas siguientes:

  • Don Lope de Cardona
  • El capitán Urrea
  • Doña Casandra Centellas
  • El rey don Alonso de Aragón
  • Don Pedro, su hijo
  • Don Bernardo de Cardona
  • Un secretario
  • Ramiro y Felis, soldados
  • Leonardo
  • Rogerio, rey de Sicilia
  • Clenarda, su hija
  • Rosinda
  • [Patrón de una tartana]
  • [Un criado]
  • [Fabricio, soldado]
  • [Lupercio, soldado]
  • [Riselo, pescador]
  • [Belardo, pescador]
  • [Fausto, pescador]
  • [Lauro, pescador]
  • [Tebano, pescador]
  • [Un paje]
  • [Felisardo, capitán]
  • [Fernando]
  • [Músico]
  • [Dos alabarderos]

NOTA: Además de la lista que aparecía en ABC se señalan entre corchetes personajes integrados por Cotarelo; sólo hemos debido añadir los tres últimos [Fernando….alabarderos].

ACTO PRIMERO

Salen con caja y bandera soldados galanes y detrás dellos don Lope de Cardona, General.

LOPE

1No paséis más adelante;Quintilla
2mejor es volver atrás
3y al honor más importante,
4pues no nos celebran más,
5en vitoria semejante.
6Volved a la mar, soldados,
7y no entremos en la tierra
8en tan mal punto llegados,
9pues que las puertas nos cierra
10cuando volvemos honrados.
11Gran señal de mal venidos,
12no alegrar nuestros oídos
13sus trompetas y atambores,
14pues nos tratan, vencedores,
15como pudieran vencidos.
16Yo hice salva en presencia
17de la hermosura del alba
18a los muros de Valencia,
19mas no responde a mi salva,
20si anda la envidia en mi ausencia.
21¿No merece la persona
22de don Lope de Cardona
23que una pieza al viento dieras
24cuando de tantas banderas,
25Patria, tus muros corona?
26Si el rey de Sicilia viene
27a vengar su hijo, y salgo

30hago que su curso enfrene,
31sino por vuestro valor,
32españoles generosos,

106Luego que con esta armadaRomance
107partiste, ilustre don Lope,
108a buscar la de Rogerio,
109que la costa a España corre
110en venganza de la muerte
111de su hijo, que una noche

113que estaba en Sicilia entonces
114-bien que, por ser en torneos
115no fue venganza conforme;
116pero la muerte de un hijo
117obliga a hacer sinrazones-;
118el mismo Príncipe, a quien
119fuiste a servir, y conoces
120por mancebo inquieto y fácil,
121todas tus obligaciones
122quiso pagar en tu ausencia,
123para que mientras le cobres

125en la suya te deshonren.
126Dio Pedro en solicitarme
127y con papeles de amores
128hizo terceras por fuerza
129a muchas señoras nobles.
130Dio en hacer públicas fiestas,
131dio en vestir de mis colores
132su persona y sus crïados.
133Yo, viendo tanta desorden,
134quejéme al Rey; mas es padre:
135no le castigó, riñole
136con más blandura que es justo,
137pues le dio licencia al doble.
138Que quien de secreto yerra,
139con temor se descompone;
140pero en viendo que se sabe,
141no hay mal a que no se arroje.
142Vino una noche, y aun muchas,
143con tantos armados hombres,
144como si a Sicilia fuera
145contra el fuego de sus montes.
146Dicen que trajo instrumentos
147de músicas y de voces,
148-pero ausentes los maridos
149son los silencios mejores-;
150dábalas tu fama al cielo
151y deste delito inorme:
152oyólas tu viejo padre,
153que descansaba en Segorbe.
154Descolgó la antigua espada,
155la que en tantas ocasiones
156fue defensa de su Rey,
157la que por entrambos cortes
158tiñó mil veces la sangre
159de los moros españoles,
160y ciñéndosela al lado,
161vino secreto a la corte
162la noche de más rüido,
163aunque es verdad que no rompen
164voces de músicas dulces
165oídos y honor de bronce.
166Metió mano el noble viejo
167sin hacer las prevenciones
168que a su Príncipe eran justas,
169aunque agravien los mayores;
170mas dicen que él no pensó
171que estaba allí, y atrevióse
172como honrado, que al agravio
173no hay razón que le reporte.
174Huyó la gente de Pedro,
175porque eran aduladores,
176y las manos y la lengua
177nunca en una mesa comen.
178Quedó Pedro con tu padre,
179y, por mi desdicha, hirióle,
180aunque tan poco, que apenas
181corrió sangre que le tomen.
182Pero era sangre real,
183que ésta aun, dicen los dotores,
184que sacarla a un Rey enfermo
185es género de traiciones.
186El rey don Alonso, airado
187contra tu padre, le pone
188en la Torre de Serranos,
189cien hombres guardan la torre.
190Esta es la causa de haber
191mandado que cuando tornes,
192cierre sus puertas Valencia,
193y que ninguno te honre.
194Los jinetes de la costa
195con el pendón de San Jorge,
196secretos están mirando
197en qué tierra los pies pones.
198Con guerra, Lope, te aguardan,
199y lo menos, con prisiones.
200Valencia se llamó Roma
201y pues fue su antiguo nombre,
202hoy querrá serlo contigo,
203y tú de sus Cipïones;
204hoy serás el Africano,
205tan vitorioso y tan pobre.

500¡Oh, qué materia tan profunda habíaOctava real

503¿Cuál hombre puede haber tan desdichado?

513¿Qué Pompeyo piadoso entre los varios

395But these are strange turns, madam; Naples hath
396No dwellings for us when we are quit of these,
397We'll with our grief make tame some wilderness.

Exeunt.

2[.1]

Enter King [of Naples], Prince, Alberto [and] Fabio.

King of Naples

398What's to be done?

Prince

What's to be done? Done! You've undone all,
399Betrayed the crown you wear! I see it tremble
400Upon your head – give such a license to
401A rebel! Trust him abroad to gather
402Strength to the kingdom's ruin!

King of Naples

Strength to the kingdom's ruin! What can such
403A naked man attempt to make us fear?

Prince

404He carries with him a whole army, sir,
405The people's love, who want no giddiness
406Had they but opportunity, and such
407A master rebel as Vittori to
408Make spoil of all. – Who counseled him to this?

Alberto

409Not I, an't please your grace: I wish it heartily
410Undone.

Prince

Undone. You wish it, sir? Are wishes now
411The remedy for such a mischief? You,
412When the state bleeds, will wish it well again;
413You're fine court surgeons! – [To the King] Had you stayed his father,
414It might have checked his treason, or Cassandra –

Alberto

415[Aside] That's his torment.aparte

Prince

[Aside] That's his torment. We had been secure.
416Exasperated now with his affront,
417As never traitor wanted impudence
418To blanch o'er his rebellion, he may inflame
419The neighbor princes to conspire some war
420For his revenge.

Fabio

For his revenge. His grace says right: there may
421Be a consequence of much danger, and Vittori
422Has fame abroad.

King of Naples

Has fame abroad. I did it for the best,
423By his absence thinking to remove his anger.
424I could have been content to have honored him
425For, to say truth, his services did challenge
426More friendly payment.

Fabio

More friendly payment. To say truth, he was
427A noble, valiant gentleman and deserved –

Prince

428What deserved he?

Fabio

What deserved he? A halter, an't shall please
429Your highness; I did wonder at your patience
430He was not put to death.

Prince

He was not put to death. I must acknowledge
431Vittori has deserved for many services
432The love and honor of his country, fought
433Their battles and brought conquest home, made tame
434The seas that threatened us, secured the land;
435And Rome allowed some consuls for less victories,
436Triumphs and statues.

Fabio

Triumphs and statues. Most excellent Prince!
437How just he is.

Prince

How just he is. But, when opinion
438Of their own merit swells 'em into pride,
439Which sets a price on that, which modesty
440Should count an act of their obedience,
441They forfeit the reward of thanks and honor
442And betray poor and most vainglorious souls.
443Scipio and Antony, and other Romans,
444Deserved well of the Senate and were honored;
445But, when they ran to faction and pursued
446Ambitious ends to undo their country's peace,
447They were no longer patriots but declared
448Rome's poison, and like gangrenes on the state
449To be cut off, lest they corrupt the body.

Fabio

450Was ever prince so wise!

King of Naples

Was ever prince so wise! But son, son, how
451Can these stains reach Vittori? He hath given
452No argument to suspect his fall from loyalty.

Prince

453I do not, sir, accuse him, nor did I,
454More than became the spirit of a prince,
455Show I was sensible of his father's impudence.
456If you remember, when I urged what trespass
457His father had committed he urged aloud,
458"Was this all my reward?", as if his service
459Were obligation to make us suffer
460And justify their affronts. But I waste breath,
461Since you are so well pleased; my duty, sir,
462Shall speak me still your son, but let me take
463Boldness to prophesy their insolence
464Struck at my person first, but you will find
465Their pride reach higher: I am but a branch
466Superfluous and may be pruned away.
467You have, you say, no argument to suspect
468His fall from loyalty; if what's done to me
469Be dead within you, yet remember now
470You have disengaged, by exile, his relation
471And tie of subject: he owes now no faith to you.
472What that, and his disgrace and opportunity
473Abroad may frame him to, I leave to imagine.

[Going.]

King of Naples

474Nay, prithee, come back, thou hast awaked me;
475I find my rashness; I did never think
476There had been so much danger. We will study
477Timely prevention, let 'em be called back,
478Fly after 'em, and in our name command –

Prince

479You sha' not need.

King of Naples

You sha' not need. How "sha' not need"?

Prince

You sha' not need. How "sha' not need"? Your pardon.
480In hope your wisdom would allow it after,
481I have made that my act: Julio is gone
482With strict commission for that purpose.

King of Naples

With strict commission for that purpose. Julio?
483I thank thy care.

Fabio

484'Twas most divinely thought on, most maturely.
485Now all your jealousies are laid.

Prince

Now all your jealousies are laid. [To the King] I shall
486Compose myself at his return to wear
487What countenance you will direct.

King of Naples

What countenance you will direct. Cassandra
488You've sent for too?

Prince

You've sent for too? By any means, she is
489So precious to Vittori. Had she sinned
490Alone to merit banishment, he would follow her
491Through all the world.

King of Naples

Through all the world. Women are strangely attractive;
492Fame speaks her virtuous too.

Prince

Fame speaks her virtuous too. Some virtue she has –

Enter Julio[, with] Alphonso guarded.

493Julio has prospered. – [To Julio] Thou'st done good service. –
494Alphonso, though your late affront to us
495Be foul in its own nature and may encourage
496Others by your impunity, yet we have
497With the remembrance of your former actions
498Lost your offense. Vittori too shall find
499The honor he deserves.

Alphonso

The honor he deserves. How's this?

Prince

The honor he deserves. How's this? Where is he?
500He does not scorn our mercy! – Julio,
501Where is Cassandra?

Julio

502Shipped with Vittori, thank Alphonso for't,
503Whom you have pardoned; they are both at sea.

Prince

504Whirlwinds pursue 'em!

King of Naples

Whirlwinds pursue 'em! Where's your son, Alphonso?

Alphonso

505Embarked with his fair mistress. – [To the Prince] I observe,
506My lord, which way your anger moves; in vain
507You vex your soul for them. The sea's no part
508Of your command, the winds are masters there,
509Which cannot raise a storm so black and ominous
510As their own country.

Prince

As their own country. By what means escaped they?

Alphonso

511Take it from me, and after cut my head off.
512I charged him, as his heart wished to enjoy
513A father's blessing as he loved the honor
514Of his Cassandra, fearing some new plot
515To hire a bark and quickly put to sea,
516Whilst I made some stay to dispose affairs
517That might befriend us in another country.
518He did obey and had my prayers, the winds
519Conveyed him swiftly from the shore, and had
520Your creature, Julio, not made such haste,
521I had dispatched and in another vessel
522Followed his ship, but heaven determined I
523Should be again your prisoner. Use your power,
524But look to give account for every hair
525Of this old head, now withered in your service.

Prince

526To the castle with him!

Alphonso

To the castle with him! Ay, there's the King. –
527[To the King] Let me use one word more, royal sir, to you.

Prince

528You'll hear him?

Alphonso

You'll hear him? Fear not, Prince, my soul's not fall’n
529So low to beg compassion.

King of Naples

So low to beg compassion. Speak, Alphonso!

Alphonso

530My duty still preserved, I would advise
531Your age to quit the trouble of your kingdom
532And ask the Prince's leave to turn a Capuchin.
533Why should you stoop with burden o'such a state
534And have a son so active? Turn friar, my lord,
535And make the youngman king.

Prince

And make the youngman king. I must endure.

King of Naples

536Away with him!

Fabio

Away with him! I'll see him safe, my lord.

[Exit with Alphonso and guard.]

Enter a Messenger.

Prince

537What hasty news with you?

Messenger

538To arms, great sir, for your defense! There are
539New dangers from the sea.

King of Naples

New dangers from the sea. Another fleet?

Messenger

540And sailing this way, we suspect they are
541Sicilians.

King of Naples

542Vittori gave a blow to their design.

Prince

543D'ye but suspect it, villain?

Julio

D'ye but suspect it, villain? It may be
544Some scattered ships.

Prince

Some scattered ships. Has not Vittori mocked us
545And played the villain with your trust?

King of Naples

546They could not be reinforced so soon. – [To the Messenger] What number?

Messenger

547They cover, sir, the seas.

Prince

They cover, sir, the seas. Gather up forces to
548Prevent the landing.

Messenger

Prevent the landing. 'Tis imposible!
549They touch our shore by this time.

King of Naples

They touch our shore by this time. Then make safe
550The city.

Alberto

551It may be another fleet, meant to relieve
552The first and came not forth so soon.

King of Naples

553Now we want Vittori.

Exit.

Prince

554All the diseases Naples ever groaned with
555O'ertake Vittori! But Alphonso shall
556Pay dearly for this mischief.

Julio

Pay dearly for this mischief. Be not, sir,
557Dejected; 'tis more easy to defend
558At home than thrive in foreign war. These men
559Will find as proud resistance.

Prince

Will find as proud resistance. Canst thou think
560I do look pale for this? No, Julio,
561Although the sudden news might move me somewhat,
562I have a heart above all fear and can
563Know no distraction but Cassandra's absence;
564That makes me look so wild and tears my brain
565With the imagination.

Julio

With the imagination. But the state
566We are in requires you should be active, sir.

Prince

567Ah, Julio, the armies which I fear
568Are not abroad, they have made entrenchment here.

Exeunt.

[2.2]

A shout within[, then] enter the King of Sicily, Horatio, Trivulsi [and] Fabrichio.

Horatio

569Though Naples do not bid you welcome, sir,
570Ashore, the joys and duties of your subjects
571Cannot be silent.

King of Sicily

Cannot be silent. We do thank you all.
572The seas were kind, and the winds kissed our sails.
573All things conspired to our revenge.

Trivulsi

All things conspired to our revenge. Your justice
574Our very enemies acknowledge it
575And, conscious of their injury, are afraid
576To look upon us.

King of Sicily

To look upon us. Marshall of the field,
577Give present order for entrenchments,
578We'll quarter here; you shall make good that part
579With your horse troops and plant cannons on that hill
580To play upon the town. Naples shall find
581We did not venture all upon one stake;
582That petty loss at sea which made them triumph
583And, perhaps, careless of more opposition
584Shall dearly be accounted for, beside
585Dishonoring our daughter and our court
586By such a rude departure.

Horatio

By such a rude departure. As they had
587Scorned your alliance.

King of Sicily

Scorned your alliance. Thy particular
588Suff'rings, Horatio, and wounds are put
589Into the scale.

Horatio

Into the scale. They are not worthy, sir.
590Had his sword reached my heart, my death had been
591No sin compared to that affront he threw
592Upon yourself and daughter. I was bound
593To engage that blood was given me to serve you,
594And I do love those drops that, in a cause
595So just, made haste to show their duty to you
596Better than those that dwell within my heart.

King of Sicily

597We are confident of thy loyalty.

Enter Rosinda and Flavia.

Trivulsi

We are confident of thy loyalty. The Princess.

King of Sicily

598Alas, Rosinda! Thou were not bred to these
599Tumults and noise of war. Has not the sea
600Impaired thy health? I was too rash to allow
601Thy travail and expose thy tenderness
602To this rude voyage.

Rosinda

To this rude voyage. It appears to me
603A pleasant change of air. I have heard men talk
604Of many horrors that attend the seas,
605Of tempests and of dangers; I have seen
606Nothing to fright me. If the waves put on
607No other shape, I could exchange methinks
608My dwelling on the land.

Horatio

My dwelling on the land. We owe this happiness
609To you, fair Princess, for whose safer passage
610The breath of heaven did gently swell our sails.
611The waves were proud to bear so rich a lading
612And danced to th'music of the winds.

Rosinda

And danced to th'music of the winds. You show
613Your complement, my lord. Call you this Naples?

King of Sicily

614The kingdom of our enemy, which shall
615Groan for the inhabitants. Are all our forces
616Landed?

Trivulsi

Landed? Safe to your wishes and expect
617What they shall be commanded.

King of Sicily

What they shall be commanded. We must first
618Secure the ground we have: being defensed
619With works, we may prevent their sallies and
620Assault to our best advantage. – Still preserve
621Thy courage, my Rosinda; 'tis for thee
622We have adventured hither.

Rosinda

We have adventured hither. And you have
623Been kind to the petition of your daughter,
624Who can in duty wait upon your fortune.
625At home, I should have withered in your absence;
626I shall grow valiant here.

King of Sicily

I shall grow valiant here. My dearest child,
627Whose very eyes do kindle flames of courage
628In every soldier, be still safe and promise
629Thyself a brave revenge.

[Exeunt all but Rosinda and Flavia.]

Flavia

630What will become of us, madam?

Rosinda

631We must take our fortunes; I am sorry
632For thee.

Flavia

For thee. You have some reason for yourself.
633If any danger follow, I know where
634To place the cause, but I dare suffer with
635Your grace.

Enter Pazzorello and Didimo.

Your grace. Pazzorello, madam, and the page.

Rosinda

636He's come in good time to relieve our thoughts.

Pazzorello

Madam.

Didimo

Come, pluck up a good heart!

Pazzorello

'Tis coming out as fast as it can. Sweet Didimo, hold my head.

Didimo

Come, 'tis but a little seasickness.

Pazzorello

"Seasickness," quotha? – A vengeance of all drunken voyages, I can do nothing but –

Rosinda

How now, Pazzorello?

Pazzorello

O madam, never did man cast up so much and had so little skill in arithmetic! Nothing grieves me, but that I have not drunk for't. I have a perpetual motion in my belly, the four winds are together by the ears in my small guts; would I had never known the sea! Little did I think – Oh –

Flavia

Thou art a freshwater soldier.

Pazzorello

Freshwater? I know not. I'll be judged by the whole ship if I was not in a sweet pickle.

Rosinda

The worst is past, this is but physic.

Pazzorello

If I had thought the sea would have given me so many vomits, I would have seen it burned ere I would ha' ventured so far! I ha' purged both ways; an the enemy had met us before we landed, I should have scoured some on 'em.

Didimo

How do you now?

Pazzorello

The fit is not so violent altogether, o'shipboard I ran a tilt; howsoever, I beseech your grace that I may go home again.

Rosinda

There is no way by land.

Didimo

And a little more jogging at sea –

Pazzorello

The very word "sea" boils in my stomach and will make my mouth run over presently – Ho! It comes, it comes!

Exit.

Didimo

Madam, I have a great desire to attend him. I have cast a plot to make your highness merry.

Rosinda

You'll play the wag with him; we'll trust you to pursue it.

Didimo

I humbly thank your grace.

Exit.

Rosinda

637Flavia, does not the day look black o'th'sudden?

Flavia

638It has not the same complexion. I hear
639A noise too.

[Storm, with thunder and lightning.]

Rosinda

A noise too. From the sea, it grows loud.

Flavia

640'Tis well we are ashore. O me! I tremble
641To think what would be come on's an we had
642Not been afore this tempest; I thank providence.
643I was upon the sea once in a storm,
644But they use to clap the women under hatches;
645I never prayed so in my life.

[Re-]enter King [of Sicily,] Horatio, Trivulsi [and] Fabrichio.

I never prayed so in my life. The King!

King of Sicily

646I know not what to think: no sooner landed
647But such a storm pursue us! Does not this
648Affright Rosinda into paleness? – Dost
649Not feel an ague?

Rosinda

Not feel an ague? I have rather cause,
650Sir, to rejoice: it overtook us not
651Upon the sea, the fury of it there
652Might have been fatal.

Horatio

Might have been fatal. Be not troubled, sir,
653My soul doth from this omen prophesy
654The victory you wish upon this kingdom,
655Nor is it superstition to believe
656That heaven doth point us out the scourge to Naples
657By seconding our coming with a tempest.
658The waves were proud to entertain our navy,
659The fish in amorous courtship danced about
660Our ship, and no rude gale from any coast
661Was sent to hang upon our linen wings
662To interrupt our wishes. Not a star
663Muffled his brightness in a sullen cloud
664Till we arrived, and then observe how heaven
665Threatens the fall of this proud enemy
666By this prodigious tempest, which but gives
667Them warning of a greater.

King of Sicily

Them warning of a greater. We are confident
668Thou hast happily expounded. What lightning
669Darts from those angry exhalations!

Horatio

670It speaks the flame of our revenge.

King of Sicily

It speaks the flame of our revenge. What thunder!

Horatio

671The loudness of our cannon; let their fears
672Apply it and run mad with apprehension.

Trivulsi

673Our ships must needs fall foul on one another,
674Riding i'th'haven.

Horatio

Riding i'th'haven. Let 'em crack their ribs,
675We have the more necessity to tug for't.

King of Sicily

676Yet would thou wert at home!

Rosinda

Yet would thou wert at home! Fear not for me, sir,
677Your absence would present my imagination
678With more affliction. I suffer less
679In knowledge and shall rise by brave examples,
680Valiant above my sex; these horrors fright
681Not me.

King of Sicily

Not me. This fire will quicken the whole army –

[Enter] soldiers, pursued by Vittori [with his sword drawn, bearing] Cassandra half dead under his arm.

682What mutiny is here?

Vittori

What mutiny is here? Base villains, to take part
683With all the malice of the world against me!

King of Sicily

684What are you?

Vittori

What are you? I am a gentleman, and dare
685Rather than suffer a rude hand divorce
686This burden from my arms: defy you all.
687Alas, she will be gone! O my Cassandra!
688Thy soul sha'not forsake thee thus, I'll take it
689In with a kiss.

Trivulsi

In with a kiss. Some whom the wreck has cast
690Upon the shore.

Rosinda

Upon the shore. Pity the gentlewoman.

Vittori

691Come not too near: the man that first attempts
692This lady had better rip his mother's womb.

King of Sicily

693Whence are you?

Vittori

Whence are you? You are strangers I perceive;
694Then I presume to tell you I have more justice
695To tread upon this earth than you or any
696The proudest. It once gave us birth, and fate,
697Ungentle fate, hath sent us back to die here,
698But I will not outlive my dear Cassandra.

King of Sicily

699Do you delight in wounds? Resign that lady.

Vittori

700Not while my hand can manage this; the blood
701You take will make us walk on even pace
702To death, and when my soul can stay no longer,
703I'll leave a curse to blast you. But if you
704Bear hearts of flesh about you and will promise
705A pity to this poor departing spirit,
706I will not use a sword but give my life
707To be commanded from me at your pleasure:
708Your care will come too late.

King of Sicily

Your care will come too late. I promise by
709The word and honor of a King she shall
710Be carefully attended.

Vittori

Be carefully attended. Though that name
711Breed wonder in me, it secures all thoughts
712That may concern her safety.

[Resigns Cassandra to the attendants.]

King of Sicily

That may concern her safety. See, Rosinda,
713With as much diligence to this lady's health
714As you'd preserve your own.

Horatio

As you'd preserve your own. An excellent creature!

King of Sicily

715My faith is past.
716Now if you please, you may acquaint us with
717Your name and quality.

Vittori

Your name and quality. [Aside.] Something on the suddenaparte
718Weighs my heart lower: I ha' not power to thank him.

King of Sicily

719Already you have expressed yourself this countryman.
720Be more particular.

Vittori

Be more particular. My name's Vittori.

King of Sicily, Horatio

721The Admiral of Naples?

Vittori

The Admiral of Naples? It was a title
722I had too late and lost it for my service.
723I cannot conjure up the dead to witness;
724There be some living that remember me.
725It was my chance to have the best at sea
726Against the bold Sicilian.

King of Sicily

Against the bold Sicilian. A chance say'st?

Vittori

727Few victories can boast more: all is but
728The die of war, which valor must obey.
729My lot was to bring peace and triumph home,
730And my reward was banishment; the sea
731Held me a sinful burden to the waves,
732Or else the blood I shed to mix with 'em
733In anger and revenge conspired to throw
734Our bark, with the distressed lading back
735Upon this flinty bosom of our country.
736You have at full my misery; be just
737To that poor lady, whatsoe'er I suffer.

King of Sicily

738Your fame was with us earlier. – Entertain him.

[Soldiers] disarm Vittori.

739You are welcome, man; there's cause we should
740Be kind to you.

Vittori

Be kind to you. Will a King stain his honor?

King of Sicily

741Know, miserable man, thy destinies
742Have made thee his, that will exact severe
743Account for many lives. – [Aside] Most happy storm! –aparte
744Thy master too shall find a punishment
745Great as his pride. – [Aside] How fortunate we are!aparte

Vittori

746I ask no mercy for myself: be kind
747To that poor lady, as you're a prince, and I
748Will kiss my fate.

King of Sicily

749We violate no promise made to her,
750Though torment make thee curse thyself. – [Aside] Blest heavens!aparte
751You shall pay dear for all.

Vittori

You shall pay dear for all. O my Cassandra,
752When at the expense of all my blood I have bought
753Thy precious life from these hard-hearted men!
754Shed one tear on me, and I am paid again.

Exeunt.

3[.1]

[Enter Didimo and Pazzorello.]

Didimo

You should have thought of this afore.

Pazzorello

I did think and do think on't again, but there was a necessity of going with the Princess or losing my place at court when she came back; prithee, sweet Didimo, counsel me, I shall ne'er endure this bouncing of guns. Happy are they that can destroy gunpowder without offense in their musterings! Soldiers may talk, but there's neither wit nor honesty in making so many cripples; yet I would give one of my legs to have the t'other secured, I care not which. Cowards are commonly creatures of understanding. Would I had purged away my soul at sea! There had been peace among the haddocks.

Didimo

Come, I have a trick to save thee harmless: thou shalt entreat to be gentleman of a company.

Pazzorello

Shall I? What's that?

Didimo

A singular privilege I can tell you; oh, the right hand file! Do not you know't?

Pazzorello

A right-handed file?

Didimo

There's no honor like it: I'll not give a rush to be an officer. Your gentleman of a company marches in the van.

Pazzorello

Van? What's that?

Didimo

The bullets first salute him, he goes up to the mouth of a cannon, he lies perdu –

Pazzorello

Perdu?

Didimo

More glory than to command an army; to lie two hours upon his belly in the field and dig a hole for his chin when the bullets whisper in both his ears, "whiz!" To be trod upon by horses and scorn to reveal himself – sometimes to be snatched up by a party of firelocks or, if he fight, to be cut into honorable collops or have his limbs strewed about the field which, found by a subtler's wife, are sod for the knapsack-men and go current for camp mutton. My father was a captain, and I have heard him tell brave stories of these gentlemen of companies.

Pazzorello

And thou wouldst ha' me one of these gentlemen?

Didimo

By any means.

Pazzorello

Have the bullets first salute me, lie perdu, as you call it, and be cut into honorable collops, or have my haunches sod by a subtler's wife and pass for camp mutton! This the preferment you wish me to, Master Didimo.

Didimo

You shall be in no danger; I have but told you what fortunes other men have met withal. You shall be secure and march in the van.

Pazzorello

And come up to the mouth of a cannon?

Didimo

'Tis my meaning.

Pazzorello

Which if I do, I'll give the cannon leave to eat me.

Didimo

Dost thou think I would advise thee any thing for thy hurt?

Pazzorello

Hurt! No, no, these are but flea-bitings to have my limbs strewed about the field, or so.

Didimo

Come, I love thee and will give thee proof. Thou hast got money in thy service; put thy body in equipage and beg of the Princess to be one of these brave fellows. I will put thee into a way to get everlasting fame, and not a hair of thy head shall be the worse for't; thou shalt come off.

Pazzorello

My head shall come off!

Didimo

Thy whole body triumphant, my Rosicleer, and live to make nations stand a tiptoe to hear thy brave adventures! Thy head shall be enchanted, and have a proof beyond the musty morion: didst never hear of men that have been slick- and shot-free, with bodies no bullets could pierce?

Pazzorello

That's by witchcraft.

Didimo

Thou'st hit the nail, boy! I will procure this feat done for thee; fear nothing, but be very secret. Thy head shall be an anvil and break all the swords that light upon't, and, for the shot, thy breath shall damp a cannon; it shall fall off like one of thy buttons.

Pazzorello

If this could be compassed, I should love witches the better while I live.

Didimo

Here's my hand. Something shall be done, but put on a brave outside of resolution for the credit on't, that the world may believe 'tis thy valor puts thee upon desperate actions from which a charm shall bring thee off, or the devil shall nay to somebody. Enter Rosinda, Cassandra [and] Flavia.
Here's the Princess. Look high, and let me hear how you'll deserve the benefit.

Cassandra

755Madam, I know not in what language to
756Express those humble thanks my soul is full of.
757It shall be justice, you command this life
758You have preserved.

Rosinda

You have preserved. We should have forfeited
759Humanity not to have relieved you
760In such distress.

Enter Horatio.

Horatio

In such distress. Shall I not trespass, madam,
761Beyond your mercy by this bold intrusion?

Rosinda

762My lord, you're welcome.

Horatio

763Your grace honors me, but to you, lady,
764I am directed.

Cassandra

I am directed. To me, noble sir?

[They walk apart.]

Pazzorello

765We shall be rusty here, for want of use.
766Oh, for an action of battery! I long
767To fight pell-mell with somebody.

Rosinda

To fight pell-mell with somebody. Pazzorello?

Didimo

768He's grown most strangely valiant.

Flavia

He's grown most strangely valiant. How he looks!

Pazzorello

Madam, I have an humble suit to your highness.

Rosinda

To me? You're like to prosper in't.

Pazzorello

I beseech you I may not be a common soldier: I would cross the seas for something. Let me be gentleman of a company, and let the bullets fly as fast as they can.

Rosinda

I must confess you ask a place of honor but of danger.

Pazzorello

Danger's an ass! Oh, that I were to fight with the General now for two crowns!

Flavia

A mighty wager!

Didimo

He means both the kingdoms.

Pazzorello

I would desire no more than my finger against his musket. If we make no assault presently against the walls, I shall go near to mutiny and kill two or three of our own captains.

Rosinda

This he that was seasick!

Pazzorello

Oh, there is no honor like to marching in the van! I'll not give a rush for a man that won't lie perdu half a year together and come up to the teeth of a cannon.

Didimo

To the cannon’s mouth; I speak by a figure.

Pazzorello

Now you talk of the mouth, I will eat every day this leaguer four-and-twenty cannon bullets buttered and, as many Spanish pikes for asparagus, their steel points will fortify my stomach. I will kill my hundred men an hour for a twelvemonth together.

Flavia

You'll not have men enough to conquer.

Didimo

When the men are all dead i'th'town, he'll lie with all the women and get as many more, rather than want enemies.

Pazzorello

Oh, how I could demolish man, woman and child now!

Rosinda

I see your spirit and must cherish it; I'll speak to my lord. You may have your desire, but be not seen in't for your honor.

Pazzorello

He's here, indeed. [seeing Horatio] – Didimo, when shall I be bewitched? An the devil do not put me in good security –

Didimo

Trust me for that; let's leave 'em about it.

[Exeunt Didimo and Pazzorello.]

Horatio

769Can you be cruel, lady, to that man
770That offers you his heart?

Cassandra

That offers you his heart? Alas, my lord!
771You ask mine in exchange, and I have made it
772A gift already to Vittori: while
773He lives, he must possess it. As you're noble,
774Prosecute this no further.

Horatio

Prosecute this no further. [Aside] I have done;aparte
775Vittori then must die.

Enter King of Sicily, Trivulsi [and] Fabrichio.

King of Sicily

Vittori then must die. Horatio,
776Command your prisoner be brought to us presently.

Horatio

777I shall, sir.

Exit.

Cassandra

I shall, sir. As you are a king, I beg your mercy
778To poor Vittori.

Rosinda

To poor Vittori. I petition too
779For her desires.

King of Sicily

For her desires. Unless he will be cruel to himself,
780His fate smiles on him. – [To Cassandra] Does he love you, lady?

Cassandra

781Great sir, we are one soul; life cannot be
782So precious as our loves.

King of Sicily

So precious as our loves. You shall preserve him. – Rosinda.

Rosinda

783I obey.

King of Sicily

I obey. Leave us. –

Exit [Rosinda].

I obey. Leave us. – Thy health
784Is but a prologue to his blessing; that
785Paper [Gives Cassandra a paper.] speaks our intention, you shall
786Present it. If he be wise, his judgment
787Will meet our purpose; what we lost at sea,
788We enable him to satisfy by a second
789Proof of his courage, and propound not only
790Life and his liberty but so great an honor
791As next our title – there is left no glory
792To equal it.

Cassandra

To equal it. You're all bounty.

King of Sicily

To equal it. You're all bounty. There are some
793Conditions: if you find him cool, you may
794Apply what argument you find to warm
795His resolutions.

[Re-]enter Horatio [with] Vittori.

His resolutions. Here he is, I leave you.

Vittori

796I wait, sir, your command.

King of Sicily

I wait, sir, your command. She will instruct you. – Horatio.

Exeunt King of Sicily and Horatio[, and then Trivulsi and Fabrichio].

Vittori

797Enjoys my best Cassandra perfect health?
798The King is just, and I have not enough
799With this poor life to satisfy –

Cassandra

With this poor life to satisfy – Vittori,
800We now begin our happiness! The King
801Has been so gracious –

Vittori

Has been so gracious – All that's good reward him!
802To see thee safe and smile, I write my ambition.

Cassandra

803When you peruse that paper, you will find
804How much we owe to providence. It was
805The King's command I should deliver it;
806The words were of such comfort that came with it,
807I must be confident you'll thank him for it.

Vittori

808What should this be?

(Reads.)

"Noble Vittori, we know you are a soldier and present you not with naked pity of your fortune. What some prince would take away we have purpose to cherish, your life; enjoy yourself, and with it the command of all our forces. Naples' ingratitude, if you have put no false shape upon your injuries, may be argument enough to your revenge and justice. Be our soldier, fight against your country so with one valor you punish them, and make us satisfaction; we will have pledge for this trust in Cassandra, whose head shall be the price of your disobedience."

809Sure I have lost my understanding, ha?
810Does it not bid me to fight against my country?
811I prithee read, Cassandra, and repent;
812Thou hast thought him merciful.

Cassandra

[Reads.] "We have pledge for this trust in Cassandra,whose head shall be the price of your disobedience."

813The language is too clear.

Vittori

The language is too clear. It carries more
814Darkness than ever the night was guilty of,
815And I look black already to have read it.
816Does he call treason justice? Such a treason
817As heathens blush at, nature and religion
818Tremble to hear: to fight against my country!
819'Tis a less sin to kill my father there
820Or stab my own heart; these are private mischiefs
821And may in time be wept for, but the least
822Wound I can fasten on my country makes
823A nation bleed and myself too, blasts all
824The memory of former actions,
825And kills the name we live by. O Cassandra!
826Thou didst not well to praise the King for this.

Cassandra

827His words did sound more comfort.

Vittori

His words did sound more comfort. Prithee tell me,
828How canst thou hope I should preserve my faith
829Unstained to thee and break to all the world?

Cassandra

830Naples has been injurious, and we made
831No solemn vow to love what hath betrayed us.

Vittori

832Take heed, and do not grieve the saints to hear thee.
833If Naples have forgot Vittori's service,
834I must not make a desperate shipwreck of
835My piety. What greater vow? It was
836Articled in the creation of my soul
837I should obey and serve my country with it
838Above myself; death is a brave excuse for't.
839No, he shall see I am a soldier
840And dare be just; say he should torture me,
841Shall wickedness be strong in punishment
842And we not be as valiant in our suffering?

Cassandra

843Can then Vittori be content to leave his
844Cassandra to the misery of life
845Alone? For in the number of mankind
846I ne'er shall find another in whose love
847I can place any comfort.

Vittori

I can place any comfort. Do not say so!
848Princes will court thee then, and at thy feet
849Humble their crowns and purchase smiles with provinces.
850When I am dead, the world shall doat on thee
851And pay thy beauty tribute; I am thy
852Affliction and, when thou art discharged
853From loving me, thy eyes shall be at peace;
854A sun more glorious shall draw up thy tears
855Which, gracing heaven in some new form, shall make
856The constellations blush and envy 'em.
857Or if thy love of me be so great that when I am sacrificed
858Thou wilt think of me, let this comfort thee:
859I die my country's martyr and ascend
860Rich in my scarlet robe of blood, my name
861Shall stain no chronicle, and my tomb be blest
862With such a garland time shall never wither.
863Thou, with a troop of wives as chaste as thee,
864Shall visit my cold sepulcher and glory
865To say "this doth enclose Vittori's dust,
866That died true to his honor and his country."
867Methinks I am taking of my leave already
868And, kissing the wet sorrows from thy cheek,
869Bid thee rejoice, Vittori is a conqueror
870And death his way to triumph.

Cassandra

And death his way to triumph. This is all
871A new disguise for grief to make it show well.

Vittori

872To make it show, indeed! I have talked idly
873And miserably forgot myself. I am checked,
874This tells me another tale: if I refuse
875To obey the King's directions, he is not
876So kind to take the forfeit of my life,
877But he will make the price of my neglect
878Cassandra's innocent blood. If I obey not
879To do an act injurious to virtue,
880Thy soul must be divorced.

Cassandra

Thy soul must be divorced. Sir, I have read it,
881And were not worthy of Vittori's love
882To value this poor life above his honor.
883Keep your high thoughts, preserve all peace within you;
884You shall not buy my breath with your own shame.
885I'll die with that devotion I ha' prayed for you,
886Which, trust me, was most heartily, and I'll shed
887No tears for my own funeral; if any
888Unruly drop break forth when we are parting,
889'Tis more to leave Vittori than the world.
890Yet if thou wilt give me leave, I'll confess to thee,
891Before my head fall from this other piece
892I would deceive the hangman; for ere thou
893Go from me, with a sigh into thy bosom,
894I would convey my spirit and leave him
895But a pale ghost to mock his execution.

Vittori

896I cannot hold, this conflict is more fierce
897Than many thousand battles. Canst thou die?

Cassandra

898If you will have it so. You have taught me
899To be in love with noble thoughts; I shall
900Have some weep o'er my hearse, and when I'm gone,
901Sealed by my blood a martyr for thy love,
902The world shall praise me for it, and the virgins
903And wives, if I obtain no other monument,
904Build me a tomb within their hearts and pay
905Their yearly songs and garlands to my memory
906That died to save Vittori's life and honor.

Vittori

907How should Cassandra die to save Vittori?

Cassandra

908Allow it
909So you be happy, and although my wishes
910Are rather for the punishment of Naples,
911More cruel than our enemies, yet if you
912Think it dishonor to oppose that country,
913I have a heart most willing to preserve
914By any death your fame. Lose not a scruple
915Of yourself for me; I carry thy love with me
916And prophesy my story shall throw more
917Disgrace on Naples than all thy revolt
918Can bring upon thy name.

Vittori

Can bring upon thy name. I am in a tempest
919And know not how to steer; destruction dwells
920On both sides.

Cassandra

On both sides. Come, resolve.

Vittori

On both sides. Come, resolve. I must – To let
921Thee live, I will take arms. – [Aside] Forgive me then,aparte
922Great Genius of my country, that to save
923Her life I bring my honor to the grave.

Exeunt.

[3.2]

Enter Fabio and Mauritio at several doors.

Fabio

I know not what to say to these garboils. There's a hot Naples toward, and the Prince is so humorous o'th'other side I dare not come near him. – Captain Mauritio!

Mauritio

Signor Fabio, you dishonor your body by straining so much complement.

Fabio

Your humble servant, Captain.

Mauritio

A court instrument, and so deep a base you forget yourself! Have the wars made this alteration? Keep your garb and be staunch, signor: a captain is a thing too coarse for your acquaintance, you won't know soldiers in peace.

Fabio

Alas, sir! The necessity of my affairs at court and place so devours my attendance that I cannot give that respect which is due to a gentleman of your quality. No neglect, I beseech you, sir.

Mauritio

I am glad 'tis come about, what do you think now of a musket bullet next your heart? 'Tis very provocative. Come, be not sad, thou mayst live a day or two longer.

Fabio

I hope, Captain, the state of the city is not so desperate.

Mauritio

We expect a battle every hour, and the walls to fly about our ears; if they should be patient, we ha' not provision to endure a siege. What will become of your pumps, signor, your wrought shirts and rich nightcaps? I say nothing of your wardrobe, jewels and other trinkets.

Fabio

I stand not upon them; my life is more precious to me than all these.

Mauritio

What pity it is, so profound a gentleman should die by gunpowder! What would you give to be saved now?

Fabio

How d'ye mean, Captain?

Mauritio

For your soul let it shift, I think thou hast little care on't thyself; there be many would give all their estate to outlive these combustions.

Fabio

I would I were sure on't, condition I lost half my land.

Mauritio

A match! My life against half your land to secure you and make an indifferent bargain presently.

Fabio

Your life? How are you sure to live?

Mauritio

If I die, you have half your land by't; if you live, 'tis worthy dividing transitory fortunes, I shall ha' the worst match on't.

Fabio

But how will you assure me, Captain?

Mauritio

Thou art not senseless! Why, your venture is but land against my life, which is more precious, I hope, than thousand acres; is not this to be considered? Clap hands, and we will have articles drawn for mutual assurances. I do not this to every man, but I hope to have good on thee hereafter. Enter King of Naples, Prince, Julio [and] Alberto.
The King!

Fabio

And Prince.

Mauritio

Let's withdraw then, and conclude 'tis a safe bargain for you, sir: if you fail, what would all your estate do you good? And then I forfeit my life; if you scape, I have but half your land.

Fabio

I understand and thank you, noble Captain.

Exeunt.

King of Naples

924Alphonso must be sent for out of prison,
925He's an experienced soldier.

Prince

He's an experienced soldier. To betray us?

King of Naples

926Now we are punished for Vittori's banishment.

Prince

927Your fear will make us cowards.

Julio

Your fear will make us cowards. Shall we make
928A sally forth?

King of Naples

A sally forth? Alberto.

Prince

A sally forth? Alberto. We'll expect more
929Advantage first, they have finished their redoubt.
930Is our river guarded with a sconce?

Is our river guarded with a sconce? On that part

No enemy can endanger us. What if you
932Tested Alphonso? He has been ever faithful,
933And we too rash.

And we too rash. Keep prudent watches, Julio,
934Something i'th'evening may be attempted.
935Death is the worst, and better fall with honor

937Were in their camp. O Julio!

Were in their camp. O Julio! 'Twere better

[Enter Fabio.]

Fabio

939A herald, sir.

A herald, sir. Admit him.

[Exit Fabio.]

King of Naples

A herald, sir. Admit him. Alberto, Julio.

Exeunt [Alberto and Julio].

[Re-]enter [Fabio], with Vittori [disguised as] a herald.

Prince

940What's the complement now?

Vittori

941Thus Naples is saluted from my master:
942Provoked by injuries above the patience
943Of kings to suffer, without thirst of blood
944Or pride of conquest, he is come in arms
945To ask a satisfaction. If you would
946Not know the fury of a war, which acts,
947Such horrid ruins 'gainst men and nature, that
948Repentance cannot easily absolve
949The guilt in them that caused it, meet conditions
950And deserve timely my great master's friendship
951With mercy on yourselves.

Prince

With mercy on yourselves. Mercy!

King of Naples

With mercy on yourselves. Mercy! Be temperate.

Vittori

952Remember , wounds are made more easily
953Than cured, and now arrived within your country,
954Revenge may spread a wild destruction.
955Let mothers still enjoy their sleep and dwell
956Within their husbands' bosom; let their children
957Live to requite the parents' groan and prosper;
958Let old men pay their debt only to nature,
959And virgins dedicate their yet chaste womb
960To Hymen's holy use, or at their choirs
961With freedom of their souls sing holy prayers
962For the sweet peace you lend 'em to serve heaven.

963This fellow's sent to mock us; in my heart
964I repent all the tie of arms and nations
965That gives such saucy freedom to a herald.

Vittori

966I claim my privilege and dare say more.

Prince

967What more?

Vittori

What more? Vittori is our general.

King of Naples, Prince

968Vittori? Dares that traitor –

Vittori

Vittori? Dares that traitor – When kings leave
969Their justice and throw shame upon deservers,
970Patience so wounded turns a Fury.

Prince

Patience so wounded turns a Fury. How!
971Dares Sicily trust him?

Vittori

Dares Sicily trust him? Yes, he has good pledge;
972Too great a pawn.

Prince

Too great a pawn. [Aside] This, this vexationaparte
973I did expect, but we must not be frighted. –
974Tell your insulting master he shall find
975Men that both dare and can resist this fury.
976Conditions we despise, nor let him magnify
977His purchase in that rebel; every soldier
978With us hath equal courage to Vittori,
979But a soul far more honest.

Vittori

But a soul far more honest. Honest?

Prince

But a soul far more honest. Honest? So, sir;
980This war shall justify upon his heart.

Vittori

981[Aside] I dare not stay to hear more, least my passionsaparte
982Betray me; what a fire this language has
983Shot through my blood! The poor old king says nothing,
984But fills a place like a state cipher.

Prince

But fills a place like a state cipher. Herald,
985Return this to that giant of your war,
986Vittori; in his absence, we shall find
987A punishment for his treason. And, to cool
988His hot veins, say the first attempt he makes
989Against us shall as valiantly be answered
990With his father's head.

Vittori

With his father's head. Ha!

Prince

With his father's head. Ha! By thy master's soul
991It shall! And this is all our answer. See
992Him safe without the walls.

Exeunt [all but Vittori].

Vittori

Him safe without the walls. Thunder has struck me!
993I feel new stings about my heart: my father?
994Was ever man so miserably thrown
995Upon despair? If I refuse their war,
996I lose my wife Cassandra; if I fight,
997My father bleeds. Some divine arm sustain
998My feeble soul, instruct it how I should
999Distinguish sorrow and which blessing rather
1000I should now part with: a dear wife or father!

4[.1]

Enter Rosinda [and] Cassandra.

Rosinda

1001But did the Prince affect thee so, Cassandra?

Cassandra

1002I have told you, madam, every circumstance;
1003I should but flatter my own misery
1004To speak it less. Misfortune had not made me
1005Your prisoner now if he had been more temperate.

Rosinda

1006But did thy heart allow him no affection?
1007Thou wert much unkind.

Cassandra

Thou wert much unkind. He had my duty, madam,
1008Which still I owe him as my prince, but I
1009Had but one faith, and that was given Vittori.
1010I fear I have displeased you.

Rosinda

I fear I have displeased you. No, thou hast not.
1011Dost think he loves thee still?

Cassandra

Dost think he loves thee still? I know not, madam,
1012But I hope not.

Rosinda

But I hope not. Would I could hope so too!
1013Thou hast deserved my confidence, and although
1014Thou canst not help me, I must tell thee all.
1015I love that Prince, loved when I first saw him,
1016And when he courted me, I thought 'twas necessary
1017To show I had a soft heart, but he flattered
1018And took too soon occasion of his absence.
1019The wounds he left upon Horatio
1020Were not so deep as mine, which howsoe'er
1021I have disguised yet from my father's eye,
1022Can find no cure without his surgery
1023That left them in my bosom; to this end
1024I urged my father to this war and begged
1025With many prayers to witness his revenge.

Cassandra

1026That was a desperate remedy. How if
1027Your father be o'ercome and you made prisoners?

Rosinda

1028We shall find death or ransom: the first would
1029Conclude my sufferings; th'other not much harm us,
1030Perhaps advance my ends. But if the victory
1031Should crown our army, I should interpose
1032To make conditions for the Prince; fate must
1033Decide one of these ways.

Cassandra

Decide one of these ways. Madam, I pity you.
1034Sure if the Prince knew with what constancy
1035Your love breathes after him, he would find a passion
1036To meet your noble flame.

Rosinda

To meet your noble flame. I know not whether
1037To pray for victory or to be conquered,
1038For till the wars conclude I must despair
1039To see whom my desires pursue.

Cassandra

To see whom my desires pursue. 'Tis possible
1040That you may see him, madam.

Rosinda

That you may see him, madam. When?

Cassandra

That you may see him, madam. When? This night,
1041And speak with him, without exposing your
1042Person to any danger.

Rosinda

Person to any danger. Prithee do not
1043Mock me, sweet friend.

Cassandra

Mock me, sweet friend. You were compassionate
1044Of me, and 'tis but duty I should answer it
1045With my desires to serve you. Not to hold
1046Your thoughts in expectation, is there any
1047Gentleman near whom you dare trust?

Rosinda

Gentleman near whom you dare trust? With what?

Cassandra

1048With carriage of a paper. I shall run
1049Some hazard, but there's nothing can weigh down
1050That goodness you have showed me, being a stranger.
1051I'll frame a letter, madam, in my name,
1052And by some charm of love invite him to
1053Your tent; if he retain part of that flame
1054Which did so command in him, be assured
1055The Prince will come.

Rosinda

The Prince will come. Thou wert create to make
1056Me blest, but with what safety can he reach
1057Thus far and not be known?

Cassandra

Thus far and not be known? He to whose trust
1058You give this secret shall remove that fear.

Rosinda

1059There is a captain –

Cassandra

There is a captain – Best of all.

Rosinda

There is a captain – Best of all. Fabrichio.

Cassandra

1060Send for him straight: if you allow this device,
1061I'll presently dispatch the amorous summons.

Rosinda

1062I'll call thee sister!

Cassandra

I'll call thee sister! Call me servant, madam;
1063In that I am honored.

Enter Flavia disguised [as a hag].

Flavia

In that I am honored. Are you ready, madam?

Rosinda

For what?

Flavia

To laugh; I am turned enchantress, and now 'tis upon the minute, Pazzorello, by the boy's directions, comes for his magical armor.

Rosinda

I have something of more consequence to finish, but I may be at the end of your mirth.

Exit.

Flavia

Prosper in all your wishes.

Enter Didimo.

Didimo

Flavia! That's excellent, Hecate never looked so dreadfully. Where's the Princess?

Flavia

She commanded not to expect her, but she'll not be long absent. Where's the gamester?

Didimo

Almost within reach of your voice. You'll remember the circumstance, that he may be capable of the charm; he's mad to be enchanted.

Flavia

I warrant you; I have some furies to assist me too. Conduct him hither. [Exit Didimo.]
If the fool after this conceiving himself bewitched should grow valiant and do wonders, who can help it? If he have but the wit to keep his own counsel, let him take his course. But he approaches.

[Re-]enter Pazzorello and Didimo.

Didimo

That is she.

Pazzorello

That old hag?

Didimo

Good words! She has come two hundred mile to day upon a distaff: salute her, she expects it.

Pazzorello

Would you have me kiss the devil?

Didimo

Do, I say. –

1064This is the gentleman, my loving aunt,
1065For whom I do beseech your powerful spells.

Flavia

1066To make him slick and shot-free?

Didimo

To make him slick and shot-free? Right, dear aunt.
1067He is a precious friend of mine, and one
1068That will be ready servant to your pleasures
1069At midnight or what hour you please to call him.

Pazzorello

Thou wouldst not ha' me lie with the old witch? What a generation of hobgoblins should we have together!

Didimo

1070Nor, for this benefit, shall you find him only
1071Obedient to yourself, but very dutiful
1072To any devil you have.

Flavia

To any devil you have. He is welcome, child.

Pazzorello

What a saltpeter breath she has!

Flavia

Where is Mephistopheles?

Pazzorello

No more devils, if you love me.

Flavia

I must have some to search him.

Pazzorello

Search me? Where? For what?

Didimo

How much was I overseen not to give you warning! Be not afraid; what have you about you?

Pazzorello

About me, where? In my breeches? What do you mean? I shall be cut for the stone.

Didimo

Have you any money about you?

Pazzorello

Yes, I have money of all complexions in my pocket.

Didimo

Away with it, as you love yourself! Not for your right hand have one piece of gold or silver about you, no charms can fasten on you then; her spells can have no power if you do not throw it away instantly – give me't, I'll keep it from her knowledge, this were a trick indeed –. Have you no goldfinches in your fob?

Pazzorello

I defy him that has anything in the likeness of coin.

Didimo

This is all money in your pocket, and come to be made shot-free!

Pazzorello

What must I do now?

Didimo

Kneel down and expect with obedience and admiration what will become on you. – [Pazzorello kneels and Didimo blindfolds him.]
Great aunt, the gentleman is clear and ready. – You are sure you have no more impediment of this nature? If you dissemble and be killed afterward, thank yourself.

Flavia

Where be my spirits?

Didimo

He humbly desires you would finish him as privately as might be: he does not know the constitution of every devil, and to make too many acquainted, if he could be finished otherwise, your art may dispense.

Flavia

He must cut off his little finger, then.

Pazzorello

How! Cut off my finger?

Didimo

What did you mean? Here's a ring, a diamond.

Pazzorello

I had forgot it.

Didimo

No more, off with't if you love your hand! Here's a jest to fool away your life quickly; not for the world present it to her. – Great lady of the Laplanders, this gentleman implores your mercy to his joints, and offering this trifle, humbly prays you would honor him to wear it for his sake.

Flavia

Comes it freely off?

Pazzorello

It came off very hard, but I beseech your learned beldamship to accept it as a token of my duty.

Joy in all bosoms! Thus our kingdoms knit.

Prince

1760Horatio, we are friends too.

Horatio

1761Own me your servant, sir. I beg your pardon.

Prince

1762I cannot ask forgiveness oft enough
1763For injuries to thee, noble Vittori,
1764Alphonso and Cassandra.

Vitttori, Alphonso, Cassandra

Alphonso and Cassandra. All your creatures.

Enter Mauritio [and] Fabio.

Mauritio

1765Justice, my lord!

[Presents a paper.]

Fabio

Justice, my lord! Mercy, my lord!

King of Naples

Justice, my lord! Mercy, my lord! What's this?

Mauritio

1766A deed of half his land if he survived
1767These wars, which are now happily determined.
1768My life was his security, which will
1769Be merrier with the moiety of his acres.

King of Naples

1770How if he had died?

Mauritio

1771His land had gone to the next heir, that's all;
1772His ghost would hardly call upon my forfeit.
1773If I had died, his land had been discharged,
1774But we, both living, must part stakes. He has
1775Enough for two on's.

Fabio

Enough for two on's. Cheated by a soldade!

Prince

1776He must confirm his act.

Fabio

1777But in such cases, sir, where men's estates –

Prince

1778Are too much, sir, and, like their talk, impertinent –
1779Go to! You're well.

Fabio

Go to! You're well. But half well, an't like your grace.

Mauritio

1780'Tis very well.

King of Naples

1781Our city spreads to entertain such guests.

Prince

1782Never was music of so many parts
1783As, friends to Naples now, we all join hearts.
